chapman_dublin.text: Chapbooks, chapbooks! Sure there's a ballad for everything. Mind the pigeons.

rail_guard.text: Connolly Station. Trains to every Irish station you've visited. Please mind the gap, the step and your dignity.
Hop aboard. The Wildlore rail runs to any town you have visited on this island. Where to?

sailor.text: Back to Holyhead, is it? The Ulysses is warming her engines, and a seagull has already bagged the best seat.

then.text: The launch was a triumph. Eleven people stayed for the cake. Nobody stayed for the speech. Metrics are metrics.
If you do come to Kilkenny, do bring the castle's measurements. I've been rounding up.

else.text: A stage on the quays. A banner reads IRELAND'S ANCIENT EAST EXPERIENCE (tm), with a smaller line underneath: terms apply. A string quartet is playing something that is nearly a reel.
Dia dhuit, Dublin! That's 'hello' for the visitors. It's in the brief. I'm told to say it with warmth.
Ireland is a land of five thousand years of heritage. And now, at last, it comes with a booking system.
Newgrange. Tara. Glendalough. Kilkenny Castle. Every stone, every ring fort, every holy well. Available in three tiers: Bronze, Silver and Ancient.
A Warden hands you a lanyard. It says GUEST on it, with a small barcode and a smaller smiley face.
The Wardstone will keep the stones quiet and presentable. No humming during the tour. No ghosts, unless pre-booked.
Her eyes land on you and narrow, like a woman checking a spreadsheet.
Oh. You. The unlicensed walker, from the incident reports. You're taller than the file said.
I won't fight you here. It's a launch. There's cake. Go and enjoy Dublin. Kilkenny, if you must. The castle would make a lovely Members' Lounge.
Slán abhaile. That's 'safe home', and I mean it. In a purely contractual sense.

then.text: Nice coat. You look like you're about to be in a film where it rains.
Happy St Patrick's Day! The Liffey's not green, that's just the light. Probably.
Halloween started here, you know. Samhain. We've been dressing up and scaring the neighbours for two thousand years.
Christmas Eve, the famous ones come out to busk on Grafton Street. I stand nearby looking famous.
Rain on the Ha'penny Bridge. Everyone's walking fast now, so I'm playing fast. Teamwork.
Sun on the Liffey! The whole city's in a good mood. Tips are up, so's the tempo.
Dusk is the best time on the bridge. The lamps come on and everyone goes soft.

bridge_busker.text: {greeting} The Ha'penny Bridge is a lovely spot to play. Everyone slows down on it, and the echo does half my work.
A halfpenny to cross, they charged. I do it for a euro and a smile. Or a smile and a euro. The smile's optional.

then.text: Grand soft day, as we say in Dublin. Perfect weather for an old library and a very old book.
You're up early! The queue for the Book of Kells hasn't even woken up yet.

kells_guide.text: The Book of Kells is a gospel written out by monks around 800 AD, with the most gorgeous illustrations: cats, mice, peacocks, and a lot of knotwork.
It is kept under glass in the Old Library. They turn a page every so often so it doesn't get bored. Honestly.

then.text: Ducks don't mind the rain. They look at me like I'm the strange one for having an umbrella.
Early breakfast for the ducks. They're very punctual. I'm the one in my slippers.

green_duck.text: These ducks know me. They know my pockets, my cardigan, and my heavy sighs.
St Stephen's Green had a different feel, once. It was a common for grazing cattle. Now it's a common for grazing sandwiches.

then.text: Paddy's Day. I've been in since nine. Breakfast was a pint and a moral victory.
Twelve pubs of Christmas. I'm on pub four. Pub four is also pub one.
Autumn. Dark at six, raining by seven, pub by half past. Grand.
That wind would take the hat clean off you. I'm just saying, mind the hat.

pub_regular.text: {greeting} Temple Bar's got more pubs per square foot than anywhere I know. I'm not recommending that, it's an observation.
Sláinte, they say, which is 'health'. It means a toast. I'm told it also means 'one more'. Both are true on the same evening.

then.text: Fog in the Phoenix Park. The deer step out of it like ghosts. Very polite ghosts.
Windy one. The deer are all huddled under the trees, giving out about it.

deer_keeper.text: The deer in the park are fallow deer, spotted in summer, and they've lived here since the 1660s. They're very relaxed.
You can walk right up to them, but I'd advise against it. They look fluffy. They're not for hugs.

fawn.text: It looks at you with the calm of a deer that has seen several hundred tourists today. You are the nicest of them.

gate_dublin_south.text: Roadworks. The M11 is being resurfaced with a heritage-compliant finish. It's very fancy tarmac.
Declan at the hurling hall says he'll sort the permits, if you win him over. Everyone in Dublin knows Declan.

gate_dublin_north.text: North road's closed for the Ancient East launch. The sign says 'Experience in progress'.
Try the long way round, via the west. You may find the closure lifts by the time you get there.

dublin_lamplighter.text: Some of the old lamps round Merrion Square are still gas, you know. Somebody's got to keep them happy.
Dublin by lamplight. The Georgian doors all glow red and blue and yellow. Like sweets in a jar.
Quiet streets, warm lamps, and a fox having a look at me. That's my night sorted.

dublin_fox_watcher.text: Dublin's full of foxes at night. They're more Dublin than I am, and I'm from Phibsborough.
Red torch, see? Foxes don't mind red light. They just carry on with their business.
Saw one trot over O'Connell Bridge last week like he was late for a bus.

isles_anju.text: {greeting} Namaskaram! I'm Anju, a nurse, from Kerala in the south of India. There are thousands of Indian nurses in Irish hospitals. Without us the night shift would be a very quiet place.
Ireland was always the country people left. Since the 1990s people come here instead: from Poland, Brazil, Nigeria, China, India, and since 2022 many from Ukraine.
My daughter has a Dublin accent, does Irish dancing and corrects my Irish. I am very proud and a little annoyed.

then.text: There are far more people of Irish descent outside Ireland than in it. Seventy million, by some counts. She's in there somewhere.
You went all that way? Then you've done more than most of my cousins.
Here. A copy of a steerage ticket, Liverpool to New York, from a museum shop. Not hers. But it could have been.

else.text: The Famine Figures here, Black '47 in Liverpool, and Annie Moore in Cork. Take your time. She did.
The Famine Figures here, Black '47 in Liverpool, and Annie Moore in Cork. Take your time. She did.
The Famine Figures here, Black '47 in Liverpool, and Annie Moore in Cork. Take your time. She did.
{greeting} I'm Maura. My great-great-grandmother walked out of Mayo in 1847 with two children, took the boat from Dublin to Liverpool and never came home. Her sister went on to New York.
Nobody wrote it down. You learn it from the gaps in the family, the names that stop.
Walk the emigrants' road for Maura?

then.text: Read the Famine Figures on the quay here, then the plaque in Liverpool for the year she landed. And in Cork they remember Annie Moore, the first through Ellis Island. Then come back and tell me.

else.text: No bother. I'll be here.

then.text: The soap is on the mantelpiece and the sandwich, I regret to say, is gone. Happy Bloomsday, whenever it is. In this house it is always 16 June.
The Martello tower at Sandycove, where the book begins, is a Joyce museum now. The stairhead is still there. So is the plump, in a sense, in all of us.

Lemon soap and a gorgonzola sandwich! Sweny's and Davy Byrne's, the two holiest shops in literature. Bloom bought the soap in the morning and the sandwich at one; you have done it in better time and with less to carry in your head.
The boater is yours, and keep the soap; it will see you through to Finnegans Wake. Yes, I said yes, I will, yes.

else.text: The soap, grand. Now the sandwich. Davy Byrne's is on Duke Street, by the Green; the barman knows what to do. Gorgonzola, mustard, a glass of burgundy. Leave the burgundy.
The chemist first. Sweny's, Lincoln Place, lemon soap, fourpence in 1904. The chemist is outside the shop there; the inside is mostly books now.

{greeting} Bloomsday! Or it will be, on 16 June, and I am rehearsing. Leopold Bloom walks Dublin for eighteen hours in Ulysses and I follow him every year in this boater, which was my father's, and his father's, and is beginning to show it.

Two errands make a Bloomsday. Bloom buys a cake of lemon soap at Sweny's chemist and carries it in his pocket all day, and at lunch he has a gorgonzola sandwich and a glass of burgundy at Davy Byrne's, because the other pub was full of men eating like animals.
Fetch me both, the soap and the sandwich, and I will give you a boater of your own. The first Bloomsday was 1954, fifty years on, and the pilgrims got drunk by the second stop. Try to do better.

then.text: Lemon soap, sweet and waxy, as Bloom says. We still sell it and people still sniff it in the doorway. The shop is run by volunteers; the prescriptions stopped in 2009 and the readings never did.
Sweny's, Lincoln Place, chemist since 1847 and never once redecorated. Bloom came in on page whatever for a cake of lemon soap, fourpence, and we have been selling it ever since.
For the Joycean in the boater? Of course. One cake of lemon soap. Smell it. Go on. That is 1904, that is.

else.text: {greeting} Sweny's. The chemist shop from Ulysses, kept just as it was, mahogany, bottles and all. Mostly we sell lemon soap and read the book aloud, a page at a time, to whoever comes in.

then.text: Gorgonzola and burgundy at one o'clock on 16 June. You would be amazed how many we do. You would be amazed how many we do in January.

Davy Byrne's, Duke Street, 'the moral pub', Bloom calls it, because the landlord did not let the talk get rough. Bloom has a gorgonzola sandwich and a glass of burgundy here and watches the flies on the window.
For the man in the boater? Gorgonzola, mustard, a bit of bread you could stand a plate on. The burgundy stays here. Rules.

else.text: {greeting} Davy Byrne's. We have been serving the same sandwich since 1904, or since 1922, depending on how literal you are feeling.
